content: Tropical ulcer, also referred to as Aden ulcer, Jungle rot, Malabar ulcer, or Tropical phagedena, is a skin lesion associated with cutaneous leishmaniasis. It is caused by various microorganisms, including mycobacteria, and is predominantly found in tropical climates. These ulcers typically develop on exposed areas of the body, most commonly on the anterolateral aspects of the lower limbs. In severe cases, they can erode underlying muscles, tendons, and even bones. The lesions often arise from preexisting abrasions or sores, sometimes originating from something as minor as a scratch. The majority of tropical ulcers occur below the knee, particularly around the ankle, though they can also appear on the arms. They are frequently triggered by minor trauma, and individuals with poor nutritional status are at greater risk. Once established, the ulcer may either stabilize as a chronic condition or progress destructively, involving deep tissue invasion, osteitis, and, in severe cases, necessitating amputation. Unlike Buruli ulcers, tropical ulcers are intensely painful. The lesions initially present as inflammatory papules, which evolve into vesicles that rupture, forming ulcers. Chronic ulcers can expand significantly and, over a period of 10 years or more, may transform into squamous epithelioma. There is substantial evidence indicating that tropical ulcers are infectious in nature. Fusobacterium ulcerans has been isolated from these lesions and is considered unique to tropical ulcers. Early-stage lesions may be colonized or infected by organisms such as Bacillus fusiformis (Vincent's organism), anaerobes, and spirochetes. In later stages, the ulcers may become infected with a variety of organisms, particularly staphylococci and streptococci. The condition has been shown to be transmissible through inoculation of material from affected patients. Tropical ulcers are often described as a disease of the poor and hungry, with improving socioeconomic conditions and nutrition likely contributing to their decline. Urbanization and the widespread use of protective footwear have also reduced the incidence of initiating trauma. However, susceptible individuals, including visitors to tropical regions, may still develop these ulcers. Outbreaks have been documented, such as one in Tanzania among barefoot sugarcane workers. The disease is most prevalent among native laborers and schoolchildren in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly during the rainy season. Contributing factors include insect bites, poor hygiene, and pyogenic infections. Males are more commonly affected than females. Geographically, tropical ulcers are found throughout the tropics and subtropics. In some regions, such as northern Papua New Guinea, they are the most common skin disease. They are also a frequent issue among the homeless in tropical countries, where exposure to the elements and unhygienic living conditions increase their risk. Open skin lesions from intravenous drug use can exacerbate the problem. Diagnosis of tropical ulcers is primarily clinical, based on physical examination and characteristic skin findings. Early treatment involves the use of antibiotics such as penicillin or metronidazole, often in combination with topical antiseptics. Nutritional improvement and vitamin supplementation are essential. Non-adherent dressings and limb elevation are recommended. Large, infected ulcers may require surgical debridement under anesthesia, and in advanced cases, skin grafting may be necessary to prevent progression to a chronic stage. In extreme cases, amputation may be unavoidable. Prevention strategies include the use of adequate footwear to prevent trauma, maintaining good general health and nutrition, and prompt cleaning and treatment of skin injuries on the legs and ankles. Improved hygiene and nutrition can also help reduce the risk of developing tropical ulcers. Complications of tropical ulcers include changes in skin pigmentation, with rare cases resulting in discoloration such as bright red, blue, green, or even orange. Deep tissue invasion, often involving bone, can lead to amputation. Chronic and recurrent ulceration are common, and in some cases, squamous cell carcinoma may develop, particularly at the edges of chronic ulcers. Additionally, tetanus can occur if tetanus bacilli enter through the ulcer.
